ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all proposed directors, shareholders, ultimate beneficial owners, natural-person customs broker nominees and persons with effective control against: (1) domestic and foreign politically exposed persons (PEPs) and close associates under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and FATF Recommendations 12 and 24; (2) the United Nations Security Council consolidated sanctions lists; (3) all New Zealand autonomous sanctions regimes under the United Nations Act 1946 and the Russia Sanctions Act 2022; (4) New Zealand Police Financial Intelligence Group and Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade watchlists; and (5) the US OFAC SDN list as a market-standard banking acceptance control. Enhanced due diligence is mandatory where any candidate is a PEP, has adverse media exposure, holds nominee shareholding interests, uses a complex ownership structure, or where the entity seeks Tax_Exempt_Zone classification.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Companies Office New Zealand – online company registry operated by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE); portal: https://companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Statutory naming is English-based. A company name must be capable of representation in Latin alphabetic characters, may include digits and permitted punctuation, and must end with 'Limited' or 'Ltd'. Te reo Māori names and macrons are accepted. Non-Latin scripts, including Chinese characters, must be transliterated into Latin characters, and a certified transliteration must be lodged with the Companies Office. Names must not be misleading, offensive, or likely to imply a false connection with the Crown, any New Zealand government department, or another entity.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Upon name rejection the applicant may file a written reconsideration request with the Registrar of Companies through the Companies Office portal within 20 working days of rejection. The request must identify the statutory ground of rejection, provide rebuttal evidence, and, where the name contains a restricted token, attach the written consent of the relevant Minister or regulator. The Registrar will issue a decision within 20 working days. If the refusal is affirmed, the applicant may either amend the name and file a new reservation, or apply for judicial review in the High Court of New Zealand under the Judicature Amendment Act 1972 within three months. No extension of the reservation window is available while an appeal is pending.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Not permissible as the sole office. A New Zealand customs brokerage company must maintain a physical registered office in New Zealand at which service of process can be effected and statutory records can be inspected, in accordance with the Companies Act 1993 and the Customs and Excise Act 2018. A virtual office, mail-forwarding address, or virtual reception service does not satisfy the physical substance requirement. A licensed corporate service provider's physical office may be used only under a formal registered-office service arrangement, with operational management and records control remaining at the brokerage's actual business premises.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: High. Quantified probability of an unannounced on-site inspection within the first 12 months after licensing is approximately 75% for a Medium_Risk_Enhanced customs brokerage operating with ACH and wire payment rails. New Zealand Customs Service and the Department of Internal Affairs may conduct unannounced physical inspections, inspect business premises, examine records, and test AML/CFT controls under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and the Customs and Excise Act 2018.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No 105): ss 12-21 (application for registration and incorporation), s 22 (company name restrictions), s 28 (constitution), s 32 (registered office), ss 53-55 (allotment of shares), ss 87-93 (register of shareholders), ss 128-137 (director duties and eligibility), ss 189-191 (board resolutions); Customs and Excise Act 2018 (Public Act 2018 No 96), Part 7 (customs broker licensing); Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (Public Act 2009 No 35), ss 33-40 (AML/CFT compliance programme for reporting entities); Income Tax Act 2007 (Public Act 2007 No 97), ss YD 2-YD 4 (residence and non-residence rules for companies).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, a division of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), operating the Companies Register (Registrar of Companies); NZBN assignment is effected through the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) portal administered by MBIE.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Electronic Application for Registration of a New Zealand Company (lodged through the Companies Register online portal), accompanied by the Company Constitution, the Consent to Act as Director form, the Notice of Registered Office, and shareholder and director particulars required by section 12 of the Companies Act 1993.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital is prescribed by the Companies Act 1993; the International Company may be validly incorporated and carry on business with a nominal share capital (e.g., 1,000 Ordinary Shares at NZD 0.01 each, totalling NZD 10.00). There is no mandatory escrow account, capital deposit, or capital verification requirement under New Zealand law. However, as a condition precedent to the customs broker licence, the New Zealand Customs Service will require the shareholder to procure a security bond or bank guarantee in the amount prescribed by the Chief Executive (commonly NZD 20,000 for a licensed customs brokerage house) pursuant to Part 7 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018; this instrument operates as the functional financial deposit for licensing purposes.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en:
FIRST BOARD RESOLUTION OF [COMPANY NAME] (the 'Company'), adopted by the initial directors by unanimous written resolution on [Date], at [Registered Office Address, New Zealand], pursuant to sections 189 and 190 of the Companies Act 1993. Quorum present: [Director 1], [Director 2].

1. SHARE CAPITAL AND SUBSCRIPTION: RESOLVED THAT the subscribers named in the Company's constitution be, and they are hereby, entered into the register of shareholders as the initial shareholders of the Company, and that an allotment of 1,000 fully paid Ordinary Shares of NZD 0.01 each (aggregate subscription price NZD 10.00) be and the same is hereby made to such subscribers, such allotment to be recorded in the register of shareholders kept pursuant to section 87 of the Companies Act 1993.

2. REGISTERED OFFICE ADOPTION: RESOLVED THAT the registered office of the Company be, and is hereby, fixed at [Street Address, City, Region, New Zealand] and that the Registrar of Companies be notified of such address in accordance with section 32 of the Companies Act 1993.

3. APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS: FURTHER RESOLVED THAT (a) [Director 1 Name] be and is hereby appointed as a director and Chair of the Board of the Company, effective immediately upon incorporation; (b) [Director 2 Name] be and is hereby appointed as a director of the Company, effective immediately; (c) [Secretary Name] be and is hereby appointed as Company Secretary with responsibility for maintaining the statutory registers of the Company; (d) [Officer Name] be and is hereby appointed as Chief Executive Officer with authority to open and operate bank accounts, to execute bonds and sureties, and to sign all applications for the Customs Broker Licence under Part 7 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018; and (e) [Licensed Broker Name] be and is hereby appointed as the licensed customs broker manager for the purposes of the customs brokerage business of the Company.

4. CONSTITUTION ADOPTION: RESOLVED THAT the constitution tabled before this meeting be approved and adopted as the constitution of the Company with effect on and from the date of incorporation, pursuant to section 28 of the Companies Act 1993.

5. BANKING ARRANGEMENTS: RESOLVED THAT the principal banking relationship of the Company be established with [Bank Name], that the bank mandate be executed jointly by the Chief Executive Officer and one non-executive director, and that authority limits, including wire-payment thresholds, be set at NZD 50,000 per transaction unless otherwise authorised by the Board.

6. TAX STATUS AND TAX-EXEMPT ZONE PROTOCOL: RESOLVED THAT the Board confirms the target classification of the Company as an International Company operating under a tax-exempt protocol, structured so that central management and control is exercised outside New Zealand, that the Company derives no New Zealand-sourced income, and that the Company will therefore not be subject to New Zealand income tax or goods and services tax on its foreign-source revenue, consistent with the Income Tax Act 2007; and FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the Company shall not establish a fixed place of business in New Zealand other than the registered office and shall not supply brokerage services to New Zealand-resident clients unless appropriate tax registration is first obtained.

7. ANTI-MONEY LAUNDERING AND COUNTERING FINANCING OF TERRORISM: RESOLVED THAT the Company, being a customs broker and a reporting entity under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, adopts the AML/CFT compliance programme and business risk assessment tabled before this meeting, appoints [Compliance Officer Name] as the AML/CFT compliance officer, and authorises the lodgment of the programme with the Financial Markets Authority and the New Zealand Customs Service as required.

8. REGULATORY FILING AUTHORITY: RESOLVED THAT the directors and the Company Secretary be, and they are hereby, jointly and severally authorised to file the electronic Application for Registration, to pay the prescribed Companies Office registration fee (NZD 103.40), to apply for the New Zealand Business Number, to apply for an IRD number of the non-resident company, and to take all such steps as are necessary or incidental to perfect the incorporation, licensing, and operational readiness of the Company.

CERTIFIED a true and correct extract of the minutes of the first board meeting of the Company held on [Date].

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Name Availability Determination and NZBN Pre-Enrolment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office – Companies Register online portal (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz) and the NZBN portal (nzbn.govt.nz)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Conduct a search of the Companies Register to confirm that the proposed company name is not identical or objectionably similar to any existing name and does not contain a restricted word requiring ministerial consent under section 22 of the Companies Act 1993. Enrol for a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) through the NZBN portal; the NZBN will become the permanent identifier of the legal entity upon registration. Obtain physical address proof for the registered office and the signed director consents required to accompany the application.
required_dossiers: First-choice proposed company name and two alternative names
NZBN enrolment application data set
Signed Consent to Act as Director forms for each proposed director
Proof of physical registered office address (lease, title extract, or utility invoice)
Passport copies and proof of residential address for each director and shareholder
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused on the ground of identity or similar confusion under section 22(3)-(5), select an alternative name and resubmit the application without an additional fee; if the Companies Office issues a query regarding director identity, provide certified copies of passports and a notarised address verification within 10 working days of the query.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Drafting of Constitution, Share Subscription Documents and Governance Instruments
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: External New Zealand-qualified legal counsel and a notary public for certification and apostille purposes
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the Company's constitution under section 28 of the Companies Act 1993, specifying the share structure, director powers, shareholder meeting rules, and the tax-exempt international company protocol. Draft the share subscription agreement, the initial register of shareholders, the First Board Resolution, and the AML/CFT compliance programme. Verify all officers against the fit-and-proper criteria of the Customs and Excise Act 2018 by obtaining police character certificates and commercial references.
required_dossiers: Draft Company Constitution (compliant with Companies Act 1993, s 28)
Share subscription agreement for the initial 1,000 Ordinary Shares
Initial shareholder register
First Board Resolution (pro forma as set out in the incorporation_legal_framework)
AML/CFT compliance programme and business risk assessment
Police character certificates for directors and the proposed licensed customs broker manager
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: This step involves no registry interface; internal remedial action applies. If a drafting defect is discovered, revised documents must be re-executed by the same execution process before lodgment. If any director is found not to be fit and proper, substitute such director by an extraordinary resolution prior to incorporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Electronic Lodgment of the Incorporation Application with the Companies Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office – Companies Register electronic lodgment platform
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Lodge the completed electronic Application for Registration through the Companies Register online portal, attaching the constitution, the registered office address, the director and shareholder particulars, and the director consents. Pay the non-refundable registration fee of NZD 103.40 (approximately USD 63.00) online. Upon acceptance, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation and allocates the NZBN automatically. The incorporation is effective on the date and time recorded on the certificate.
required_dossiers: Completed electronic Application for Registration
Company constitution in PDF format
Registered office address declaration (with jurisdiction: New Zealand)
Directors' first and last names, dates of birth, and residential addresses
Shareholders' names, addresses, and number of shares subscribed
Signed Consent to Act as Director forms
Evidence of payment of the NZD 103.40 registration fee
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is placed in a 'queried' status due to incomplete data, the prescribed correction period is 15 working days from notice; amend and resubmit the discrepant fields. If the Registrar declines registration, the applicant may apply for judicial review of the Registrar's decision under the Companies Act 1993 and the High Court Rules 2016, or simply re-lodge with corrected particulars.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Tax, AML/CFT and Statutory Registrations
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD / Te Tari Taake) and Financial Markets Authority (FMA), together with the New Zealand Customs Service for AML/CFT information exchange
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply to the Inland Revenue Department for an IRD number as a non-resident International Company (application form IR 596), providing the Certificate of Incorporation and confirmation that the company derives no New Zealand-sourced income; determine whether a nil-return income tax registration is required. As a customs brokerage house is a reporting entity under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, finalise and submit the AML/CFT compliance programme and business risk assessment to the Financial Markets Authority, appoint the AML/CFT compliance officer, and record the medium-risk enhanced due diligence tier applicable to the brokerage's target payment rails (Automated_Broker_Interface_ACH and wire transfers).
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation issued by the Companies Office
IRD number application (form IR 596) for non-resident companies
AML/CFT compliance programme approved by the Board
AML/CFT business risk assessment (medium-risk enhanced tier)
AML/CFT compliance officer appointment letter
Entity governance chart showing beneficial ownership
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the IRD queries the non-resident tax-exempt classification, submit an affidavit and supporting board minutes evidencing that central management and control is exercised outside New Zealand. If the FMA issues a risk-rating or governance deficiency notice, respond with a remedial action plan within 20 working days and implement agreed corrections; a failure to remedy may lead to FMA enforcement, which can be mitigated by voluntary disclosure and corrective filing.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Customs Broker Licence Application under Part 7 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Customs Service (Te Mana Ārai o Aotearoa) – Customs Brokers Licensing Team, Wellington
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: File the application for a Customs Broker Licence, naming the licensed customs broker manager and furnishing proof of successful completion of the New Zealand Customs Broker Examination, fit-and-proper declarations for all principals, a certificate of incorporation, the AML/CFT programme, and a security bond or bank guarantee executed in favour of the Customs Service in the amount prescribed by the Chief Executive (typically NZD 20,000 for a standard brokerage house). Pay the licence application fee prescribed under the Customs and Excise (Fees and Remissions) Regulations. Upon grant, the licence authorises the company to carry on the business of customs clearance brokerage and bonded transit management, and the company must ensure that every customs entry submitted to the Customs Service is certified by a natural person who is a licensed customs broker.
required_dossiers: Customs Broker Licence application form (CBL-01)
Certificate of Incorporation of the International Company
New Zealand Customs Broker Examination results for the designated broker manager
Fit-and-proper declaration and police clearance certificates for all directors
Security bond / bank guarantee instrument in favour of the New Zealand Customs Service
Board resolution authorising the licence application and bond execution
Evidence of AML/CFT registration and compliance programme submission to the FMA
Detailed corporate governance and shareholding chart
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Where the application is queried, the Licensing Team will issue a notice of deficiency; respond within 20 working days with supplementary information. If the licence is declined on fit-and-proper grounds, the applicant may request reconsideration by the Chief Executive under Part 7 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018, with a further right of appeal to the Customs Appeal Authority and thereafter to the High Court of New Zealand.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Physical Premises, Fire Safety and Occupational Health Clearance
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ); WorkSafe New Zealand; local Territorial Authority / Building Consent Authority; New Zealand Customs Service (for any Customs-Controlled Area or bonded transit depot)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: For the business premises of the customs brokerage house, obtain a Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) confirming compliance of fire safety systems, a Fire and Emergency New Zealand fire plan approval certificate, an electrical safety certificate, and a WorkSafe compliance statement under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015. If the company operates a bonded transit depot or temporary storage facility, apply separately to the New Zealand Customs Service for approval of the premises as a Customs-Controlled Area (CCA), and submit to the relevant Regional Council any environmental discharge assessment required for the storage of goods. Secure the physical premises with access controls appropriate to the medium-risk AML/CFT classification.
required_dossiers: Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) for fire safety systems
Fire and Emergency New Zealand fire plan approval certificate
Electrical safety certificate and structural load inspection report
WorkSafe health and safety policy and workplace compliance statement
NZCS Customs-Controlled Area approval (if a bonded transit depot is operated)
Environmental discharge assessment / resource consent application (if applicable)
Premises access-control and security policy
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the fire inspection identifies non-compliant life-safety items, remediate and request re-inspection within 30 days. If the local authority refuses the building consent or the CCA approval, the applicant may appeal to the relevant statutory appeal body; for resource consent refusals, appeal lies to the Environment Court under the Resource Management Act 1991.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: New Zealand Customs Service (Te Mana Ārai o Aotearoa) – Customs Brokers Licensing and Customs-Controlled Area approvals; WorkSafe New Zealand; Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ); Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand and the relevant Regional Council as the Resource Management Act 1991 consent authority
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Customs Broker Licence issued under Part 7 of the Customs and Excise Act 2018 (plus a Customs-Controlled Area approval if bonded transit or temporary storage premises are operated)

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) New Zealand, with consenting functions exercised by the relevant Regional Council and Territorial Authority under the Resource Management Act 1991
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Category 4 – Exempt / Registration (office-only customs brokerage): a full Environmental Impact Assessment is not warranted for an administrative brokerage office. Should the company operate bonded transit management facilities or a Customs-Controlled Area involving the physical storage of goods, the activity will be classified as a Discretionary Activity requiring resource consent from the Regional Council where discharges to land, water, or air, or traffic effects, exceed the permitted activity thresholds of the applicable regional plan.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Wastewater: compliance with the Resource Management (National Environmental Standards for Air Quality) Regulations 2004 and the regional plan discharge limits; where a discharge consent is granted for a bonded storage facility, typical thresholds are biochemical oxygen demand (BOD5) of not more than 20 mg/L and total suspended solids of not more than 25 mg/L. Volatile organic compounds: fugitive emissions from an office environment are negligible, but any fumigation activity within a customs-controlled area must comply with the Hazardous Substances (Hazardous Property Information) Notice 2017 and the National Environmental Standard for Air Quality. Waste handling: all controlled and hazardous waste arising from brokerage or transit operations must be transported by a licensed waste carrier and documented with controlled waste records (CWRs) in accordance with the Waste Minimisation Act 2008 and the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act 1996.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) issued by the local Building Consent Authority verifying fire safety and means of escape; Fire and Emergency New Zealand fire plan certificate pursuant to the Fire and Emergency New Zealand Act 2017; WorkSafe occupational health and safety registration and workplace clearance under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, including a structural load inspection of any storage mezzanine, electrical installation certificate, emergency evacuation plan, and an on-site first-aid and hazard management register suitable for the medium-risk AML/CFT classified brokerage house.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Inland Revenue, Te Tari Tāke) – official portal www.ird.govt.nz and myIR (secure online filing system); New Zealand Customs Service (NZ Customs) for customs broker licensing and Trade Single Window (TSW) registration
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Determine whether the foreign International Company (CK_IC) is 'carrying on business' in New Zealand; a licensed customs brokerage house requires a local presence which creates a taxable New Zealand nexus. Step 2: If the company is not incorporated in New Zealand, apply for an IRD number using form IR742 (Non-Resident Company Application for IRD Number). A New Zealand-registered company automatically receives an IRD number upon incorporation through the New Zealand Companies Register. Step 3: Submit the certificate of incorporation, constitution, certified identification documents for directors and beneficial owners, and a New Zealand address for service. Foreign companies must also register as an Overseas Company on the Companies Register if establishing a place of business. Step 4: After the IRD number is issued, register for GST through myIR within 21 days if the NZD 60,000 compulsory registration threshold is exceeded, or voluntary registration is sought to claim input tax credits. Step 5: Apply for a Customs Broker Licence under the Customs and Excise Act 2018 and obtain a Customs Client Code / Trader Registration on the Trade Single Window portal, which requires the IRD number.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a 'check-the-box' classification regime. Relevant elections and statutory mechanisms include: (i) Look-Through Company (LTC) election under subpart HB of the Income Tax Act 2007 (limited to close companies with 5 or fewer counting owners who are individuals or trustees); (ii) Consolidated group election under subpart FM (80% common ownership) allowing a group of NZ-resident companies to file a single tax return; (iii) GST grouping election under section 55 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985; (iv) Hybrid and branch mismatch elections under subpart FH (BEPS measures) to align NZ tax treatment with hybrid transfer pricing outcomes; (v) Non-resident company election to compute and file NZ branch accounts and claim deductible expenditure against NZ-source income; and (vi) the conduit election under the NRWT rules to reduce non-resident withholding tax on outbound dividends derived from underlying foreign income. For a customs brokerage house, an election to zero-rate offshore transport-related services may be made under the GST Act if statutory documentation requirements are satisfied.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST (Goods and Services Tax) – Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 (a person is required to register for GST when the total value of supplies, including zero-rated supplies, exceeds NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period; anyone supplying goods or services in New Zealand may voluntarily register if below the threshold; registration is mandatory before a customs brokerage can claim input tax credits on costs such as port fees, system charges and professional services)
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping or continuous transaction control (CTC) mandate is imposed by Inland Revenue for GST. E-invoicing is voluntary in New Zealand and operates on the Peppol interoperability framework (managed by Inland Revenue) for B2B electronic invoice exchange. However, all customs declarations — import and export — must be lodged electronically through the New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window (TSW); customs brokers must use the Automated Broker Interface or direct-to-TSW integration and each export declaration receives a Unique Consignment Reference (UCR). Peppol e-invoicing does not replace the statutory GST return filing obligations under the GST Act.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating of GST applies to: (i) goods physically exported from New Zealand by the supplier within 28 days of the time of supply (GST Act 1985, s.11(1)(a)–11(1)(c)); (ii) services supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed and where the services are supplied for the non-resident's business carried on outside New Zealand (s.11A); and (iii) goods entered into a bonded warehouse for export or transported offshore under customs bond. A licensed customs brokerage house may zero-rate its fees when the immediate recipient is a non-resident located outside New Zealand and the brokerage services directly relate to export logistics, customs clearance of offshore cargo, or documentation for goods to be exported from New Zealand. The zero-rating of services is subject to the 'directly in connection with land or goods in New Zealand' exception, so pure export facilitation services must be distinguished from services that benefit a person in New Zealand. There is no statutory 180-day foreign exchange repatriation deadline under New Zealand law; the 180-day parameter in this dossier is an internal compliance benchmark adopted by the brokerage model.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration lodged through the NZ Customs Trade Single Window (containing the Unique Consignment Reference), or the applicable re-export or temporary export declaration
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill (ocean or air) evidencing physical export of the goods from New Zealand
Outward remittance certificate or bank credit advice showing receipt of export sale proceeds into the New Zealand bank account of the supplier
Copy of the taxable supply information (GST invoice) marked zero-rated, together with IRD-endorsed export evidence (e.g., port of loading, vessel/voyage report, bond release documents)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue can redetermine GST liability and recover any incorrectly claimed zero-rating as GST debt (s.79, GST Act 1985), with use-of-money interest accruing from the original due date. Shortfall penalties under the Tax Administration Act 1994 apply: up to 20% for lack of reasonable care, up to 40% for gross carelessness, up to 75% for an abusive tax position, and up to 150% for evasion or fraudulent intent. Criminal prosecution may be brought under s.143A (imprisonment up to 5 years) and s.143B for aiding and abetting evasion. NZ Customs separately imposes penalties under the Customs and Excise Act 2018 for false or misleading export declarations (up to NZD 20,000 per offence), forfeiture of goods, and suspension or revocation of a Customs Broker Licence under s.283 for professional misconduct. Inland Revenue and NZ Customs operate a Joint Border Management System (JBMS) and use risk-profiling algorithms to scrutinise zero-rated export claims, including cross-matching export declarations with foreign exchange receipts and GST returns.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (Te Pūtea Matua), Wellington. Exchange-control powers originate from the Exchange Control Act 1953, which is currently dormant following the 1984 liberalisation of the New Zealand financial system; the Governor-General may re-activate such controls only by Order in Council on national-interest grounds. In ordinary commercial practice, the Reserve Bank performs no transaction-level FX approval function; its active role is confined to monetary policy, prudential regulation of registered banks under the Banking (Prudential Supervision) Act 2013, balance-of-payments statistics, and supervision of real-time gross settlement through the Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a freely floating exchange-rate regime with full convertibility on both current and capital accounts. There is no central-bank approval for trade-related current payments, customs brokerage commissions, dividend remittances, interest payments, or equity injections. The only outward-investment screening relevant to a non-resident owner is under the Overseas Investment Act 2005 for sensitive land and strategic assets, which is not engaged by the ordinary operation of a licensed customs brokerage house. Profit and capital repatriation to the Cook Islands International Company parent is unrestricted by FX controls but remains subject to New Zealand non-resident withholding tax under the Income Tax Act 2007 (statutory default 30% for dividends and interest, reducible only where a recognised double-tax agreement supplies a lower rate; the New Zealand-Cook Islands relationship rests on administrative cooperation and information exchange, not a comprehensive dividend-rate treaty).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: No statutory timeline and no mandatory conversion ratio exists for export receipts or export-related service fees. The surrender-and-repatriation machinery of the former exchange-control regime was dismantled in 1984 and is not in force; a customs brokerage house in New Zealand may retain international service fees and duty-fund replenishments in any convertible currency, net them against overseas disbursements, or convert at market rates without Reserve Bank consent. The sole compliance overlay is transactional: reporting for balance-of-payments statistics by the settlement bank and originator/beneficiary identity verification of international wire transfers under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, with prescribed transaction-reporting obligations triggered for cash-equivalent transactions of NZD 10,000 or more.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Capital Escrow Account (Customs Duty Deferral Bond Cash Collateral)
Capital Escrow Account (Deferred Duty Guarantee Facility)
Operational Account (Trade and FX Settlement Hub)

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Low-Medium, with material legal constraints. Offshore digital EMIs such as Wise, Airwallex, and Ebury are usable only as supplementary payment-rail facilitators, not as settlement banks or custody platforms for a licensed customs brokerage. An EMI accepting deposits or executing payments in New Zealand must either hold a registered-bank licence under the Banking (Prudential Supervision) Act 2013 or, if a non-bank deposit taker, a licence under the Non-bank Deposit Takers Act 2013; the fallback model is registration as a financial service provider on the FSP register under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 and compliance as a reporting entity under the AML/CFT Act 2009, with settlement effected through a locally registered partner bank. Holding client duty deposits or brokerage fee flows in an unlicensed EMI would breach the customs broker's fiduciary agency duties to importers and would not satisfy the New Zealand Customs Service security requirements governing deferred duty arrangements.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical appearance of directors is not an absolute statutory mandate under the AML/CFT Act 2009, but New Zealand tier-1 banks apply a de facto in-person interview policy for non-resident offshore corporate clients with tax-exempt status. For the Cook Islands International Company structure, the bank will normally require at least one authorised signatory or the registered agent's responsible compliance officer to attend an in-branch interview in Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch, carrying original or certified apostilled corporate records. Purely remote account opening is available only for low-risk entities whose directors and beneficial owners are natural persons from lower-risk jurisdictions and whose identities can be verified end-to-end through banking-grade video KYC; for the CK_IC structure, a face-to-face interview and a 15-to-25-business-day onboarding cycle constitute the realistic baseline.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cook Islands International Company with tax-exempt status and nominee or corporate directors presents a shell-company and undisclosed-beneficial-owner underwriting flag.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Provide (a) the Certificate of Incorporation and the Register of Directors and Shareholders; (b) a Certificate of Good Standing issued by the Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission within 60 days of application; (c) the registered agent's due-diligence file fully disclosing the natural-person beneficial-ownership chain; (d) the New Zealand Customs Broker Licence and ANZSIC/ISIC registration evidencing operational substance; (e) a signed beneficial-ownership declaration supported by notarised passports of all directors and ultimate beneficial owners; and (f) a source-of-funds and source-of-wealth statement corroborated by a bank reference from the Cook Islands parent's settlement bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Recurring inbound wires from the offshore parent in rapid succession to fund duty disbursements, which may be characterised as suspicious layering of international payments.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Maintain a customs-entries ledger reconciled with the New Zealand Customs Service (CUS-S and Joint Border System) showing each duty payment, tariff classification, assessment reference, and deferred-duty account statement; append signed client brokerage contracts, the New Zealand Customs client deferred-duty agreement, and MT103/purpose-code evidence demonstrating that each wire represents either a brokerage fee receivable or a replenishment of the duty escrow account; obtain an external accountant's independent verification of the fund-flow mapping from offshore parent to duty account to Customs.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Exposure to counterparties in high-AML-risk or FATF grey-listed jurisdictions within the exporter/importer client base of the brokerage house.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Prepare a transaction-boundary memorandum identifying each high-risk counterparty and its commercial rationale; supply the underlying export/import declarations, bills of lading, airway bills, and customs release records; evidence enhanced customer due diligence conducted on each such client; and demonstrate the brokerage's compliance programme includes sanctions screening against the United Nations, OFAC, European Union, and New Zealand consolidated sanctions lists for every cleared consignment.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: The Cook Islands parent (CK_IC) injects equity or extends a subordinated shareholder loan to the New Zealand brokerage treasury account via SWIFT MT103 for commercial payment cover or MT202 for interbank cover. The receiving tier-1 bank codes the credit under the Reserve Bank balance-of-payments reporting framework (BPM6 categories E1 for direct-investment equity and E49 for intercompany loans); no prior exchange-control approval is required. The AML/CFT monitoring process requires a supporting board resolution, a source-of-funds breakdown, and a cash-flow purpose statement identifying whether the funds capitalise working capital or the customs-duty escrow base. The Overseas Investment Act 2005 notification threshold is not triggered because the injection finances a licensed customs brokerage operation rather than sensitive land or strategic assets.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Customs duty payments to the New Zealand Customs Service are made through the automated broker interface of the Joint Border System, using BECS/ACH direct debit or the broker's deferred-duty escrow account that the bank operates. Overseas disbursements to vendors, foreign customs agents, and logistics correspondents are cleared through SWIFT MT103 (GPI-enabled) with MT202 cover and appropriate purpose codes under the BPM6 framework, such as P801 (transactional trade) or P811 (payments for goods). Documentary credit settlements for bonded merchandise are conducted under UCP600 with MT700/MT710 issuance and negotiation through the bank's trade finance desk. Domestic NZD balances settle same-day in central-bank money through the Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS), giving the brokerage final and irrevocable settlement for its duty-deferral obligations.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable FX Forwards (outright USD/NZD and AUD/NZD forwards matched to confirmed trade settlement dates)
FX Swaps (two-legged spot/forward combinations for short-term working-capital currency conversion)
Cross-Currency Interest Rate Swaps (CCIRS) for hedging long-term shareholder-loan and duty-deferral funding exposure
Plain-vanilla FX Options (calls and puts) permitted for non-speculative hedging of large brokerage fee receivables and disbursement pipelines

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) are effectively unavailable for NZD because the currency is freely convertible; requesting NZD NDFs would raise a speculative-trading compliance objection under FMA conduct rules.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return (Confirmation Statement) under the Companies Act 1993
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 1 month after the anniversary of the company's incorporation date each year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failed submission triggers NZD 10,000 fine for the company and each director; continued non-filing for two consecutive years may result in administrative strike-off from the New Zealand Register

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Financial Statements and Annual Report (where the company is a 'large' entity or required under the Financial Reporting Act 2013)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registrar of Companies, New Zealand Companies Office (electronic filing) and/or shareholders at the Annual Meeting
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 5 months after the company's balance date; filing with the Registrar (if applicable) within 20 working days after completion
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Director liability for non-compliance; fines up to NZD 10,000 under the Financial Reporting Act 2013; persistent default may support disqualification proceedings

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Customs Broker Licence Annual Renewal / Compliance Attestation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Customs Service (Licensing and Assurance Unit)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: On or before each licence anniversary date; typically 31 March if aligned with Customs licensing calendar
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Suspension or revocation of the customs broker licence; inability to perform licensed customhouse work; further civil penalties under the Customs and Excise Act 2018

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: AML/CFT Annual Compliance Report and Review
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Customs Service (supervisor of customs brokers under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No fixed statutory date; report must be updated and internally reviewed annually, with the review completed within 1 month of the annual balance date, and submitted to the supervisor upon request
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Fines up to NZD 200,000 for non-compliance; formal warnings; suspension of AML/CFT compliance programme accreditation; the Customs Service may suspend the customs broker licence if AML obligations are persistently unfulfilled

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A statutory audit is compulsory for the company in any financial year in which it is not 'small' under the Financial Reporting Act 2013, i.e., it exceeds at least two of: total assets NZD 60 million (USD 36 million), total revenue NZD 30 million (USD 18 million), and 50 or more full-time employees. The company is also audited if it qualifies as a 'reporting entity' under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 or is otherwise required by its governing constitution or shareholders.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: New Zealand Equivalents to International Financial Reporting Standards (NZ IFRS); small and medium companies may adopt NZ IFRS Reduced Disclosure Regime (NZ IFRS RDR) or the simplified reporting framework for qualifying smaller entities (XRB A1, PBE).

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: There is no annual public filing of ultimate beneficial ownership (UBO) in New Zealand. However, the directors must confirm the accuracy of the company's shareholding and director details on each annual return. As a reporting entity under the AML/CFT Act, the customs brokerage house must maintain a verified UBO register and conduct a periodic review at least annually, updating records upon any share transfer or change of control. The annual return must identify any ultimate holding company and significant shareholders.

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory tax holiday or preferential zone deduction is available under New Zealand income tax law for an International Company. The 'Tax_Exempt_Zone' classification does not correspond to a New Zealand statutory exemption; all New Zealand-source income derived by a resident or non-resident carrying on business through a fixed establishment in New Zealand is assessable at 28%. R&D tax credit incentives apply only to qualifying and approved R&D operations, not to a customs brokerage shell entity.
corporate_income_tax_regime.tax_loss_carryforward_limit_years: Unlimited (no statutory expiry subject to the shareholder continuity test under Subpart IA of the Income Tax Act 2007)

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 (Company Income Tax Return) and IR4S (Shareholder Information Schedule) via Inland Revenue myIR electronic filing portal
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Standard balance date of 31 March: e-filed returns must be lodged by 7 July in the same income year; paper returns by 7 July; returns filed by a tax agent generally carry a later IRD due date. Non-standard balance dates: filing is due six months and seven days after the balance date.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Company identification: legal name, IRD number, incorporation number, and nominated agent details
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter New Zealand IRD registration ID; non-resident intermediaries must have a New Zealand tax agent and apply for an IRD number before submitting the IR4

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross business income: customs clearance fees, brokerage commissions, bonded transit handling fees, and logistics service revenue
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Report only income attributable to the New Zealand permanent establishment; do not net off pass-through customs duties or GST

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total business deductions: customs duty advances, warehousing costs, forwarding sub-contracts, software, and related-party charges
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Cross-border related-party charges must be supported by transfer pricing documentation and be at arm's length

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net business income or loss before adjustments: calculated from Lines 2 and 3
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Verify arm's-length net margin in line with the TP study; avoid showing artificially low New Zealand margins

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation and tax adjustments: non-deductible expenditure, exempt income, and adjustments for prior-year losses
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident shareholders must claim treaty-related adjustments only where an approved non-resident withholding rate certificate is held

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Dividends and other non-business income received, including fully imputed dividends and interest
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Gainful non-resident shareholders must separately report NRWT liability on outward distributions

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income or loss after adjustments
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: PE income must not be shifted offshore unless the transfer pricing file proves the substance and functions of the foreign entity

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax payable at 28%: calculation of company income tax on Line 7
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use 28% corporate rate; non-resident companies do not get a reduced rate; provisional tax credits under Boxes 9 and 10 must match payments made through electronic payments

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax credits: resident withholding tax, provisional tax paid, and foreign tax credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Attach overseas tax credit evidence and DTA certificates where applicable

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net refund or terminal tax due
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Terminal tax for non-standard balance dates is due on the following 7 February; late payment triggers UOMI interest

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: NZD 250 initial penalty plus NZD 250 per day for continuing non-filing, capped at NZD 1,000; late payment penalty: 1% transitional penalty plus an incremental penalty of up to 4% under New Zealand's staged penalty regime; UOMI interest is charged quarterly. Deliberate failure to file or a false return triggers a shortfall penalty of up to 150% of the tax shortfall and potential criminal prosecution.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 30% non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) on dividends paid by a New Zealand company to non-resident shareholders; no general exemption applies for an International Company. Under an applicable DTA the rate is usually reduced to 15% for portfolio holdings and to 5% or less for substantial shareholdings (typically at least 10% to 25% voting control, depending on treaty; fully imputed dividends paid to an Australian resident can be exempt under the New Zealand-Australia DTA protocol).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: The non-resident shareholder must obtain a current tax residency certificate (TRC) from its home jurisdiction tax authority and provide it to the New Zealand payer together with a completed beneficial ownership declaration. The payer applies to Inland Revenue using Form IR290 and may obtain an approved non-resident withholding rate (ANR) determination. The treaty-reduced rate must be applied at source before payment; if the TRC and treaty documentation are not held at the time of payment, the statutory 30% NRWT must be withheld and the excess is recoverable only by a refund claim to IRD. IRD audits treaty claims and may require confirmation from the foreign tax authority.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory NRWT on interest: 15%; statutory NRWT on royalties: 15%. Treaty rates: interest is frequently reduced to 10% under the New Zealand double tax agreements (for example NZ-US, NZ-China, NZ-Japan); royalties are commonly reduced to 10% or 5% depending on the treaty and the type of intellectual property (NZ-China industrial royalties 10%; NZ-Australia copyright royalties 5%). In the absence of a treaty, gross 15% applies.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Master File and Local File will be required when the New Zealand customs brokerage entity has aggregate related-party cross-border transactions exceeding NZD 10 million in an income year and the multinational group has consolidated turnover above NZD 40 million. Country-by-Country Reporting threshold: multinational group with consolidated group revenue of at least NZD 1.127 billion must file CbC reports with IRD.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not apply the Caribbean-style Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) by name, but Inland Revenue applies a substance and control analysis: a non-resident-owned International Company purporting to be tax-exempt must demonstrate genuine economic presence in New Zealand, including real premises, operational employees, bank accounts, board functions, and the ability to make day-to-day customs brokerage decisions. Without such substance, IRD will treat the entity as having a permanent establishment in New Zealand, assess income at 28%, and may invoke anti-avoidance provisions to re-characterise the structure.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: A customs brokerage house accepting cash, wire transfers, or Automated Broker Interface instructions from non-resident principals, shell beneficiaries, or unknown cargo owners without performing CDD, beneficial-ownership identification, source-of-funds verification, or suspicious transaction reporting required under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Civil penalties up to NZD 2 million per reporting entity and pecuniary penalties for officers; regulatory sanctions include cancellation or suspension of the AML/CFT registration, public censure, and criminal fines in aggravated cases. Customs brokerage falls within the reporting-entity net and failure to register is itself a criminal offence.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior managers are treated as officers and may be prosecuted personally for failing to ensure compliance; individuals face fines and imprisonment of up to two years, court-ordered disqualification, civil restitution, and travel bans where there is a material flight risk or risk of leaving New Zealand to avoid enforcement.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Knowingly undervaluing bonded or transit goods, misclassifying goods under the Harmonized System, falsifying Automatic Broker Interface declarations, or using false import documentation to reduce duty and GST liability for a non-resident principal.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Customs and Excise Act offences: goods forfeiture; monetary penalties up to three times the duty evaded; criminal fines of up to NZD 1 million or five times the duty value, whichever is higher; imprisonment for a term up to five years; revocation of customs broker authorisations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who direct, participate in, or conceal false customs declarations are primary offenders rather than protected corporate agents; they face joint and several civil restitution for the duty shortfall, personal criminal conviction, imprisonment for up to five years, and New Zealand courts may issue travel bans or border alerts against departing principals.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Avoiding arm's-length pricing on brokerage fees, management fees, royalties, or interest flows routed through a related offshore entity so that the New Zealand customs brokerage company books artificially low or consistent losses while the non-resident counterparty retains the economic profit; absence of functional analysis and contemporaneous TP documentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: IRD will adjust the taxable income using the arm's-length principle, apply shortfall penalties of between 20% and 150% of the tax shortfall, charge UOMI interest, and may impose disclosure-related penalties for failure to produce contemporaneous documentation. Fraud factors increase penalties to the maximum level.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who sign false English-language transfer pricing policies or issue invoices that divert profits from New Zealand PE are exposed to personal liability as knowing participants in a transaction structured to defeat tax; civil recovery may extend to personal bank accounts, and serious evasion gives rise to criminal penalties and director disqualification.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends, deemed dividends on liquidation or share buy-backs, royalties, or interest cross-border to non-resident shareholders without withholding statutory NRWT or without holding a valid TRC and treaty documentation supporting a reduced rate; routing payments through a conduit account in an intermediate jurisdiction that lacks governance substance.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The New Zealand company is personally liable for the un-withheld NRWT at the statutory rate (30% dividends, 15% interest/royalty); shortfall penalties of up to 150% of the unpaid tax can be imposed, plus UOMI interest; criminal prosecution is available where the avoidance was deliberate.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Limited liability does not shield a director who knowingly causes the company to omit withholding; civil recovery can be enforced against a director as an aider and abettor of an arrangement whose dominant purpose is to defeat an NRWT obligation, with personal criminal liability resulting in imprisonment of up to five years and travel restrictions pending prosecution.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company and Economic Substance Abuse
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using a New Zealand International Company that is labelled 'Tax_Exempt_Zone' but has no employees, no office, no separate bank account, and no management decision-making authority, while the actual business of customs brokerage is conducted from a foreign trust or non-resident corporate principal, thereby claiming to fall outside New Zealand taxation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: IRD treats the entity as a resident company and PE, weighs all facts under the general anti-avoidance rule, re-characterises the Monday transactions, taxes the attributed profit at 28%, adds shortfall penalties of up to 150%, and may confiscate assets through the Proceeds of Crime Act for money laundering involved in the sham.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of both the New Zealand IC and the foreign principal can be held as parties to the avoidance scheme; the corporate veil can be pierced for sham arrangements, leaving personal assets open to civil claims; criminal conviction carries imprisonment for up to five years, director disqualification, and court-imposed travel bans.
